doc.title: Earl Watkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Slim Jenkins' club, bebop repertoire and Kenny Dorham
summary: The quartet plays bebop and backs singers at Slim Jenkins in Oakland; Ernie Royal leaves for Los Angeles.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: What would your songlist have consisted of them? Kinds of tunes?
Oh we would do bebop then. We’d were beboppers. We’d do “Now is the Time” and oh just Bird and Diz tunes.

And then of course, then as time went on we’d do ballads and we’d do standards, and when we went to Jenkins he had singers, so we’d back singers, so whatever the singer had we’d back it. And then of course since singing started to become popular so we would try to do some of the Nat King Cole things that he did at the time. [sings] Straighten up and fly right, you know. And we’d do well it was a mixed variety. And so then while we were at Jenkins we looked up in the audience and there was this guy with a trumpet in his hand and he came by and said, “Geez you guys I sure like what you do, geez I sure like what you do.” So it turned out to be Kenny Dorham. His parents had sent him out here to clean up, because he was a—

Yeah. So he used to come in to Jenkins to listen to us. So one time we did — Ernie knew who he was, I didn’t. Because that was very, very early. But anyhow once we found out who he was then — I don’t know how long he was here because we were at Jenkins maybe for about three months or maybe even longer. So then that job ended so then Ernie said, “Well, Earl, I think it’s time for me to go back to Los Angeles.” His brother Marshall was there and Marshall recorded with Eddie Heywood and traveled with Eddie Heywood’s group, and Marshall was also with this — he played piano and arranged and was a vocal coach. He coached Lena Horne and Dorothy Dandridge and — it’s on the tip of my tongue. Anyhow Marshall — so Ernie went back to Los Angeles. And sure enough, as soon as he got back to L.A. he started to work. He was with Kenton, then he got with Woody Herman and came up here with Woody’s band and went all over the country with Woody. And he ended up in Europe. He settled in Europe for a while then he ended up in New York doing studio work and everything. But anyhow Ernie left and then there was just Curtis and I, so this is 194 — late ’46, early ’47. Oh by the way, during that period too, before we went to Jenkins, we played at the Swing Club in Oakland. Now that was a club on Lower Seventh Street It’s now the site of the main post office.
